title: Balanced trees (concept only)
learn: why BSTs degrade to O(n), AVL rotations, red-black trees idea, B-trees/2-3 trees for disks. Explain-level only, no problems
hook: "What happens if the BST becomes skewed?" is a standard follow-up to any BST answer. You won't code an AVL tree in an interview, but explaining rotations and why databases use B-trees shows real depth.

explain.prompt: Explain why a plain BST can degrade to O(n), and how self-balancing trees like AVL or red-black trees prevent it.
keyPoints: inserting sorted data into a plain BST makes a chain (height n), so operations become O(n)
self-balancing trees keep height O(log n) by rotating after inserts and deletes
a rotation is an O(1) local change of a few pointers that keeps the BST ordering
AVL: subtree heights differ by at most 1 (stricter, faster lookups); red-black: looser rules, fewer rotations (used in TreeMap / std::map)
B-trees / B+ trees keep many keys per node to minimise disk reads (database indexes)
